posts.title: On leaving the city before it leaves you
posts.subtitle: What eleven years of mornings taught me about staying put, and the week I finally didn’t.
posts.content:
![Morning light on a balcony](/_pg/img/window/11/960/640.jpg)

The balcony faced east, which meant the first hour of every day belonged to it. I wrote there through three winters and one very long spring, and somewhere in the fourth year I noticed that the light had started arriving before I did.

That is the whole essay, really. The rest is me trying to work out when a place stops being where you live and becomes where you are from.

## The inventory

When I finally decided to go, I made a list of the things I would miss. It was shorter than I expected, and stranger: the bakery that closed at eleven because the owner liked to swim; the woman on the fourth floor who practised the same four bars of Satie every evening and never, in eleven years, got past them; the sound the tram made on the bend by the river, a sort of iron sigh.

Nothing on the list was a person I would lose. Everyone I loved could be visited. What I was leaving was a set of rhythms, and rhythms, it turns out, do not travel.

> Nothing ends. It just stops being yours.

My neighbour said that when I told her, handing me a jar of quince jam through the gap in the door as if she had been waiting for the occasion. I have thought about it more than anything anyone else said to me that year.

![Morning light falling across a balcony railing and a plant pot](/_pg/img/window/11/960/640.jpg "The balcony on the last morning. The plant stayed.")

## What staying costs

People talk about the courage it takes to leave. Fewer talk about the slow, quiet cost of staying past the point where a place is still teaching you anything. I had become very good at my city. I knew which side of the street stayed cool in August and which café would let me sit for three hours on one coffee. I had stopped being surprised, and a writer who has stopped being surprised is in some trouble.[^1]

So I made a second list, of the things I would not miss:

-   The version of me who answered “same as ever” when anyone asked what was new.
-   Knowing, to the minute, how long every errand would take.
-   The feeling that the year had already been written and I was only reading it back.

---

I left on a Tuesday, on the early train, with two bags and the jam. The light came up over the river as we crossed it, the way it always had, and for the first time in years I was not there to meet it. It did not seem to mind.

[^1]: A friend who edits novels says the same about characters: once they stop being surprised by their own lives, the book is over.

posts.title: Three kinds of quiet
posts.subtitle: A library, a snowfall, and the minute after an argument.
posts.content:
There is the quiet of a library, which is a held breath shared by forty strangers. There is the quiet of snow, which is not silence so much as a lowering of the whole world’s voice.

And there is the quiet after an argument, which is the loudest of the three.

posts.title: Lisbon, in the week of the heat
posts.subtitle: Shutters down at noon, the river the colour of tin, and a city that simply refused to hurry.
posts.content:
![Rooftops of Lisbon in afternoon light](/_pg/img/city/3/960/640.jpg)

By Wednesday the pavements were too hot to stand on for long, so everybody moved through the city in short, deliberate hops between patches of shade.

Nobody complained. Complaining would have taken energy, and energy was the one thing the week had made precious.

posts.title: A bus driver who waves at dogs
posts.content:
The number 207 has a driver who lifts one hand from the wheel for every dog on the pavement. Not for people. Only dogs.

I have ridden that bus for a year now and I still don’t know his name, but I know he has never missed one.

posts.title: Rereading Stoner at forty
posts.subtitle: The saddest book I know turned out to be about something else entirely.
posts.content:
![A shelf of worn books](/_pg/img/books/8/960/640.jpg)

At twenty I read it as a tragedy. At forty I read it as an argument for paying attention.

The plot has not changed. I have.

posts.title: The kitchen table as a unit of time
posts.subtitle: Every table I’ve owned has measured a different part of my life.
posts.content:
![Cups and a bowl of lemons on a wooden table](/_pg/img/table/21/960/640.jpg)

The first was a door on two trestles. The second came from a school that was closing and still had a name carved into its underside.

You can tell a lot about a year by what it left on the table.

posts.title: A ferry to nowhere in particular
posts.subtitle: Forty minutes each way, fog on both banks, and nothing to do but look.
posts.content:
![A small ferry crossing in fog](/_pg/img/fog/9/960/640.jpg)

I bought a return ticket without looking at where the boat went. That was the point.

Halfway across, the fog closed behind us and the far bank had not yet appeared, and for ten minutes the ferry was the only thing in the world.

posts.title: Receipts
posts.subtitle: A shoebox of them, kept for tax reasons, turned out to be a diary.
posts.content:
Two coffees, one croissant, a Tuesday in March. I remember exactly who the second coffee was for.

I have kept the box, though the tax office no longer needs it.

posts.title: Against the productive walk
posts.subtitle: A walk with a purpose is just a commute with better shoes.
posts.content:
Somewhere along the way walking became exercise, and exercise became something to measure.

I would like to propose the opposite: a walk that counts nothing, arrives nowhere, and is over when it is over.

posts.title: Why I stopped taking notes on trains, and what I lost
posts.subtitle: Eleven notebooks of other people’s conversations, abandoned in a single week.
posts.content:
For years I wrote down what strangers said on trains. Then I realised I had stopped listening to the people I was travelling with.

I miss the notebooks. I do not miss who I was when I kept them.

posts.title: The books I lie about having read
posts.subtitle: A confession in four titles, and one I finished out of spite.
posts.content:
Everyone has a list. Mine starts with a Russian novel and ends with a book about bees.

The spite one was worth it.

posts.title: What the tide tables don’t tell you
posts.subtitle: Numbers for the height of the water, none for the mood of the town.
posts.content:
![Low sun over a wide grey sea](/_pg/img/sea/14/960/640.jpg)

The tables give you times and heights. They say nothing about the hour when the boats sit crooked in the mud and the whole harbour smells of rope.

That hour is the one worth planning around.

posts.title: Notes from a town with one traffic light
posts.subtitle: It has been red for six years. Nobody stops.
posts.content:
![Fields at the edge of a small town](/_pg/img/field/4/960/640.jpg)

The light was installed after a meeting nobody remembers, for a crossing nobody uses.

It is the most beloved object in town.

posts.title: Salt
posts.content:
My grandmother kept salt in a wooden box by the stove, and took it by the pinch, never the spoon.

I have tried to measure a pinch. It cannot be done.

posts.title: Why our p99 doubled after the connection-pool change
posts.subtitle: A shared pool, a batch job, and nine days of looking at the wrong dashboard.
posts.content:
In March we replaced one connection pool per worker with a single shared pool of 64 connections in front of PgBouncer. Throughput went up by about a fifth. Two weeks later our p99 on the checkout path had doubled, and nothing in the dashboards said why.

This is the write-up: what changed, how we found it, and the one-line fix that turned out to be the least interesting part.

## The change

Each worker used to open its own `pgxpool` with eight connections. With 40 workers that meant 320 server connections at peak, most of them idle. The new setup shares one pool per host:

```
pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, &pgxpool.Config{
    ConnConfig:        connCfg,
    MaxConns:          64,
    MinConns:          8,
    MaxConnIdleTime:   30 * time.Second,
    HealthCheckPeriod: 15 * time.Second,
})
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("configure pool: %w", err)
}
```

On paper this is strictly better: fewer connections, better reuse, less memory on the database.

## What the traces showed

Every slow request spent 40–180 ms inside `pool.Acquire()` before running a query that took 3 ms. The pool was not too small on average. It was too small for about 400 ms at a time, whenever the batch export woke up and took 50 connections for long-running reads.

| Configuration | p50 | p99 | Acquire wait (p99) | Server connections |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per-worker pools | 18 ms | 94 ms | 0.2 ms | 320 |
| Shared pool, 64 | 15 ms | 211 ms | 162 ms | 64 |
| Shared pool + export pool | 15 ms | 81 ms | 0.4 ms | 80 |

## The fix

Give the batch export its own small pool, so it can never starve interactive requests:

```
-- Also cap it on the server side, in case someone reuses the wrong pool.
ALTER ROLE export_worker CONNECTION LIMIT 16;
```

> A shared resource needs a shared understanding of who is allowed to hold it, and for how long.

## What we changed in how we work

1.  Every pool exports its acquire-wait histogram, not just its size.
2.  Batch jobs get their own pool and their own database role.
3.  Load tests include one noisy neighbour, on purpose.

The fix was one line of SQL and twelve lines of Go. Finding it took nine days, most of which went into dashboards that measured the wrong thing.

posts.title: TIL: \watch in psql re-runs the last query
posts.subtitle: A poor engineer's dashboard, in one backslash command.
posts.content:
If you end a query with `\watch 2` instead of a semicolon, psql runs it every two seconds.

```
SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state \watch 2
```

It is my favourite way to watch a migration or a queue drain.

posts.title: How VACUUM actually decides what to clean
posts.subtitle: Visibility maps, the xmin horizon, and why one idle transaction can bloat a table.
posts.content:
VACUUM can only remove a dead row once no running transaction could still see it.

```
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age, state
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

One forgotten `BEGIN` in a psql session holds back the horizon for the whole cluster.

posts.title: TIL: context.AfterFunc
posts.subtitle: Run cleanup when a context is cancelled, without a goroutine per request.
posts.content:
Go 1.21 added `context.AfterFunc`, which registers a function to run once the context is done.

```
stop := context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() {
    conn.Close()
})
defer stop()
```

It replaced a surprising number of hand-rolled goroutines in our codebase.

posts.title: The queue that lost 0.01% of messages
posts.subtitle: An at-least-once system, an at-most-once consumer, and a retry that wasn't.
posts.content:
The broker delivered every message. Our consumer acknowledged before processing, so a crash in between dropped the work.

```
msg := <-deliveries
if err := handle(msg); err != nil {
    msg.Nack(false, true) // requeue
    continue
}
msg.Ack(false)
```

Moving the acknowledgement after the side effect fixed it, and exposed three handlers that were not idempotent.

posts.title: Histograms, not averages
posts.subtitle: Slides and notes from my talk at a regional SRE meetup.
posts.content:
The mean latency of a service is a number that describes no request that ever happened.

```
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
```

The talk walks through three incidents where the average looked fine and the histogram did not.

posts.title: TIL: git bisect run
posts.subtitle: Let a script find the commit that broke the build.
posts.content:
`git bisect run` takes a command and uses its exit code to decide good or bad.

```
git bisect start HEAD v2.4.0
git bisect run go test ./payments/...
```

It found a regression across 340 commits in eleven minutes.

posts.title: Timeouts, all the way down
posts.subtitle: Why a 30-second client timeout and a 60-second server timeout are a bug.
posts.content:
Each layer should time out slightly before the layer that called it, or work keeps running after nobody is waiting for it.

```
deadline, _ := ctx.Deadline()
budget := time.Until(deadline) - 50*time.Millisecond
```

We now set budgets from the edge inward and pass the remaining budget along with every call.

posts.title: A DNS TTL of 86400 seconds
posts.subtitle: The failover worked. The clients didn't notice for a day.
posts.content:
Our database failover moved the primary in 40 seconds. Half the clients kept talking to the old address until the next morning.

```
dig +noall +answer db-primary.internal
```

The record had been created years ago with a one-day TTL and never revisited.

posts.title: TIL: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
posts.content:
Adding `BUFFERS` shows how many pages a query read from cache and from disk.

```
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
```

It is the fastest way to tell a slow plan from a cold cache.

posts.title: Brown butter tomato galette
posts.subtitle: Serves 4 · 1 hr 10 min. The trick is salting the tomatoes an hour ahead.
posts.content:
![Sliced tomatoes in a bowl](/_pg/img/bowl/3/960/640.jpg)

This is the galette I make every week from late July until the tomatoes stop. It asks for very little: good tomatoes, bought pastry, and an hour's patience while the salt does its work.

![Sliced tomatoes in a white bowl](/_pg/img/bowl/3/960/640.jpg "Salting the slices draws out the water that would otherwise soak the pastry.")

## Ingredients

-   500 g ripe tomatoes, a mix of sizes, sliced 5 mm thick
-   1 tsp flaky salt
-   1 sheet all-butter puff pastry (about 320 g)
-   60 g butter
-   2 tbsp Dijon mustard
-   A handful of basil and thyme
-   1 egg, beaten, for the edges

## Method

1.  Lay the tomato slices on a rack, salt them, and leave for an hour.
2.  Brown the butter in a small pan until it smells of hazelnuts. Let it cool a little.
3.  Heat the oven to 200°C. Roll the pastry onto a lined tray and spread the mustard, leaving a 3 cm border.
4.  Pat the tomatoes dry, overlap them on the mustard, and spoon over half the brown butter.
5.  Fold the border over, brush with egg, and bake for 35–40 minutes until deep golden.
6.  Finish with the rest of the butter and the herbs.

> If the pastry is pale underneath, give it five minutes on the oven floor.

It keeps for a day, but it has never had to.

posts.title: Low-sugar strawberry jam
posts.content:

Keep it in the fridge once opened and eat it within a month.
